Worry? Dread? Oh, no, no, it's not like I'm having a panic attack or anything like that. I don't feel like the sky is falling or that the store is going to burn down. It's not a fearful feeling at all, really. I mean, sure, I want things to go right because I take pride in my work—I've been managing teams for over fifteen years, and I like a tight ship. But when I'm standing there with the morning crew—usually it's Dave from electronics, Sarah from apparel, and maybe one or two of the new part-timers—and I'm trying to give them the game plan for the day... I don't feel scared or worried about the future. I'm not dreading what's going to happen. It's just... I know exactly what needs to be done. I see the whole plan in my head. It's frustrating, certainly. Extremely frustrating. It makes me feel embarrassed, like I look foolish in front of my own staff, you know? But it's not dread. I'm not standing there thinking something terrible is about to happen to me or to them. I'm just standing there thinking, "Come on, Frank, just say the sentence. Just tell Dave to take the pallet jack to aisle four." But instead, it comes out all jumbled, like I'm trying to talk around a mouthful of marbles. So, no, it's not an overwhelming worry or apprehension about the future. It's just an overwhelming frustration with my own mouth in that exact moment.

So, no, there's no obvious physical reason why my thoughts are suddenly getting all tangled up like this. It just sort of... started happening on its own, without any warning or any changes in my routine. I wish it was as simple as a new medication causing a side effect, because then I could just stop taking it and go back to normal, but unfortunately, that's just not the case. It's just my brain doing this... this weird thing all by itself.\n\nDoctor: When your mind is racing and you're trying to explain things to your team, do you find yourself feeling a sense of overwhelming worry, dread, or apprehension about the future or about things going wrong?\n\nPatient: Worry? ========== OUTPUT [patient] ==========
Well, that’s exactly it, doctor, that’s actually the main reason I finally decided I needed to come in and see somebody about this. I originally thought it was just the stress of the retail environment, you know? Because it definitely happens at the store. I'll be standing there trying to explain the inventory numbers for the new quarter, or maybe I’m just trying to lay out the weekend schedule for the floor staff—which is always a headache anyway because nobody ever wants to work the Sunday morning opening shift—and the words just get entirely derailed. 

But then I realized it’s not just work. It’s happening everywhere, even when I'm completely relaxed. I’ll start out trying to talk about something simple, and then my words start jumping all over the place without my permission. I’ll go from talking about the delivery trucks we're expecting, and then that makes me say something about Thursdays, because Thursday is when the big freight truck comes in, but then suddenly I'm talking about the church grill—we have this massive, heavy-duty charcoal grill we use for the parish summer fundraisers, I've been manning it for a decade—and then before I can even catch myself, I'm going on about my boss’s tone of voice from a conference call he ran three weeks ago. 

It just leaps from one thing to the next. Trucks to Thursdays to the church grill to my boss's tone, all strung together in the same breath like it's supposed to make perfect sense. And whether it's my employees by the stockroom doors or my own family at a Sunday barbecue, they all do the exact same thing. They just stop, and they stare at me, and they get this deeply confused look on their faces... people just look at me like they absolutely can’t follow what I’m saying. It’s like they're trying to read a map that's been put through a paper shredder. So, no, it's definitely not just when I'm under pressure at the store. It's happening when I'm just trying to have a normal, relaxed conversation, too, and it's making it nearly impossible to just sit down and talk to people without feeling like I'm speaking a foreign language.

Well, "the quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog"—I mean, I could probably say that right now without a hitch. Let's see... "The quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog." See? Clear as day. But, doctor, with all due respect, that’s just a memorized trick from middle school typing class. It's when I have to explain the actual inventory numbers for the store, or when I'm trying to lay out that weekend schedule for the staff. 

I know I keep bringing up those same examples, but it's just the absolute perfect illustration of how bad this has gotten. I'll start out talking about the schedule, and then, just like I was explaining a minute ago, my words start jumping entirely on their own. They jump from the schedule to the delivery trucks, to Thursdays, to that heavy charcoal church grill, all the way to the exact tone of voice my regional manager used on a call three weeks ago. It's a total cascade. And I can see it happening in real-time because the people I'm talking to—they just freeze. They look at me like they absolutely cannot follow what I’m saying. They get this blank, concerned stare like I've suddenly started speaking Greek. 

So, sure, the fox and the dog are perfectly fine. My mouth can handle that. But if you ask me to explain my actual day to you, or manage my team, that's when the train comes completely off the tracks.

In fact, just the other day, I was looking for my favorite pen—it's this blue Pilot G2, 0.7 millimeter, the only kind I like to use for signing off on the delivery manifests because the ink flows so nicely and doesn't smudge on that cheap carbon paper they use. Anyway, I thought I'd lost it, but I closed my eyes and retraced my steps perfectly. I remembered exactly where I'd set it down: right next to the cash register on register three, right after I helped ring out a customer who was buying three packs of those AA batteries that we had on sale on the endcap. \n\nAnd appointments, I never miss those. I have my dentist appointment next Thursday at 3:15 PM, Dr. Henderson over on Maple Street, and I've had that written in my planner for six months. I even know that my car registration is due on the 14th of next month. So, no, keeping track of things isn't the issue at all. \n\nAnd as for finding words for things... no, I know exactly what everything is called. I know a stapler is a stapler, a pallet jack is a pallet jack. The words themselves are all there, sitting right in my head, clear as day. It's just... it's just what happens when I try to string them all together into a sentence that makes sense to somebody else. The words are fine, the memory is fine. It's the... the traffic control in my head, I guess you could call it. That's what's broken. But remembering where I put my keys or my glasses? No, I've got a system for that. Keys go in the ceramic bowl by the front door—the one my sister got me from her trip to Santa Fe back in 2018—the very second I walk in the house. The last time I had any kind of real physical issue was... oh, gosh, it must have been three years ago when I pulled a muscle in my lower back trying to lift a display case that was way too heavy for one person. But that healed up just fine after a few weeks of physical therapy and some muscle relaxers they gave me at the time. \n\nAnd as for new medications, no, nothing new there either. I take a multivitamin, too, just a generic one from the pharmacy down the street, the one with extra vitamin D because I don't get out in the sun much working retail all day. \n\nBut no new pills, no changes to my diet, no falls, no bumps on the head. So, no, there's no obvious physical reason why my thoughts are suddenly getting all tangled up like this. It just sort of... started happening on its own, without any warning or any changes in my routine. I wish it was as simple as a new medication causing a side effect, because then I could just stop taking it and go back to normal, but unfortunately, that's just not the case. It's just my brain doing this... this weird thing all by itself.\n\nDoctor: When your mind is racing and you're trying to explain things to your team, do you find yourself feeling a sense of overwhelming worry, dread, or apprehension about the future or about things going wrong?\n\nPatient: Worry? Trucks to Thursdays to the church grill to my boss's tone, all strung together in the same breath like it's supposed to make perfect sense. It's happening when I'm just trying to have a normal, relaxed conversation, too, and it's making it nearly impossible to just sit down and talk to people without feeling like I'm speaking a foreign language.\n\nDoctor: When you try to write down your thoughts or tasks in your planner, do you find that your writing also becomes jumbled and disorganized, or is it only your spoken words that seem to get tangled?\n\nPatient: Writing it down? No, no, it's nothing physical like that. My tongue and my lips, they work perfectly fine. I've been a retail supervisor for years, you know, managing the floor, handling the team, making sure everything runs smoothly. But recently, when I try to sit down and explain the inventory numbers for the week, or... or even just go over the weekend schedule with the staff, it's like my brain just takes off in a dozen different directions at once. \n\nI'll start talking about the stock levels, and then suddenly I'm talking about the delivery trucks, which reminds me that Thursday is usually a heavy delivery day, but Thursday is also when we have the church grill out back, and then I start thinking about the way my boss sounded when he asked me about the grill last week—his tone was just... off, you know? And before I know it, I'm trying to explain all of this at the same time, and the words are just jumping from the trucks to Thursdays to the church grill to my boss's tone, and I look up and... well, my team is just staring at me. They have these blank looks on their faces, like they can't follow a single word I'm saying. It's frustrating because it all makes perfect sense in my head, but when it comes out, it's like a tangled ball of yarn and they just... they don't get it. And it's really starting to become a problem on the floor, you know?\n\nDoctor: Aside from the trouble staying focused at work, have you been feeling unusually energetic, or like you need much less sleep than normal lately?\n\nPatient: Energetic? Oh, no, no. Definitely not energetic. If anything, Dr. Smith, it's quite the opposite when it comes to my physical energy. You see, being on the retail floor all day at my age—I'm 59 now—it really takes a toll on the joints. I'm on my feet from the moment I clock in. Well, technically I get there about fifteen minutes early, around 7:15 AM, just to walk the perimeter and check the endcaps before the doors open, but by the time I get home at night, I am absolutely wiped out. I have this brown leather recliner in my living room, great lumbar support, and the second I sit down in it, I just deflate like an old tire. \n\nSo there's certainly no unusual burst of energy going on. And as for sleep... well, I definitely still need my sleep. I try my hardest to get my full eight hours every single night. Sometimes it's hard to drift off right away because my mind is doing that... that tangled yarn thing I was just telling you about, spinning around the inventory and the schedules and my boss, but I really *want* to sleep. I crave it. I certainly don't feel like I can just skip it or run on fumes. \n\nIf I get anything less than seven hours, I'm dragging my feet the whole next day. Like last Tuesday, the neighbor's golden retriever was barking at all hours—nice dog usually, but he just wouldn't quit at the fence—and I only got maybe five hours of rest. I was utterly exhausted by noon on Wednesday, just drinking coffee after coffee in the breakroom. So, no, I haven't noticed needing less sleep at all, or feeling super energized. I just feel like a regular, tired guy who can't get his words straight when he needs to.\n\nDoctor: Have you noticed any problems with your memory, such as forgetting where you put things, losing track of appointments, or having trouble finding the right words for common objects?\n\nPatient: Memory? No, no, my memory is... well, it's sharp as a tack, honestly. I haven't been losing things or missing appointments. Anyway, I thought I'd lost it, but I closed my eyes and retraced my steps perfectly. I have my dentist appointment next Thursday at 3:15 PM, Dr. Henderson over on Maple Street, and I've had that written in my planner for six months. I even know that my car registration is due on the 14th of next month. So, no, keeping track of things isn't the issue at all. \n\nAnd as for finding words for things... no, I know exactly what everything is called. Keys go in the ceramic bowl by the front door—the one my sister got me from her trip to Santa Fe back in 2018—the very second I walk in the house. The last time I had any kind of real physical issue was... oh, gosh, it must have been three years ago when I pulled a muscle in my lower back trying to lift a display case that was way too heavy for one person. But that healed up just fine after a few weeks of physical therapy and some muscle relaxers they gave me at the time. \n\nAnd as for new medications, no, nothing new there either. I take a multivitamin, too, just a generic one from the pharmacy down the street, the one with extra vitamin D because I don't get out in the sun much working retail all day. \n\nBut no new pills, no changes to my diet, no falls, no bumps on the head. It just sort of... started happening on its own, without any warning or any changes in my routine. It's happening when I'm just trying to have a normal, relaxed conversation, too, and it's making it nearly impossible to just sit down and talk to people without feeling like I'm speaking a foreign language.\n\nDoctor: When you try to write down your thoughts or tasks in your planner, do you find that your writing also becomes jumbled and disorganized, or is it only your spoken words that seem to get tangled?\n\nPatient: Writing it down? Sometimes it's hard to drift off right away because my mind is doing that... that tangled yarn thing I was just telling you about, spinning around the inventory and the schedules and my boss, but I really *want* to sleep. I crave it. I certainly don't feel like I can just skip it or run on fumes. \n\nIf I get anything less than seven hours, I'm dragging my feet the whole next day. Like last Tuesday, the neighbor's golden retriever was barking at all hours—nice dog usually, but he just wouldn't quit at the fence—and I only got maybe five hours of rest. I was utterly exhausted by noon on Wednesday, just drinking coffee after coffee in the breakroom. So, no, I haven't noticed needing less sleep at all, or feeling super energized. I just feel like a regular, tired guy who can't get his words straight when he needs to.\n\nDoctor: Have you noticed any problems with your memory, such as forgetting where you put things, losing track of appointments, or having trouble finding the right words for common objects?\n\nPatient: Memory? No, no, my memory is... well, it's sharp as a tack, honestly. I haven't been losing things or missing appointments. In fact, just the other day, I was looking for my favorite pen—it's this blue Pilot G2, 0.7 millimeter, the only kind I like to use for signing off on the delivery manifests because the ink flows so nicely and doesn't smudge on that cheap carbon paper they use. Anyway, I thought I'd lost it, but I closed my eyes and retraced my steps perfectly. I remembered exactly where I'd set it down: right next to the cash register on register three, right after I helped ring out a customer who was buying three packs of those AA batteries that we had on sale on the endcap. \n\nAnd appointments, I never miss those. I have my dentist appointment next Thursday at 3:15 PM, Dr. Henderson over on Maple Street, and I've had that written in my planner for six months. I even know that my car registration is due on the 14th of next month. So, no, keeping track of things isn't the issue at all. \n\nAnd as for finding words for things... no, I know exactly what everything is called. I know a stapler is a stapler, a pallet jack is a pallet jack. The words themselves are all there, sitting right in my head, clear as day. It's just... it's just what happens when I try to string them all together into a sentence that makes sense to somebody else. The words are fine, the memory is fine. It's the... the traffic control in my head, I guess you could call it. That's what's broken. But remembering where I put my keys or my glasses? No, I've got a system for that. Keys go in the ceramic bowl by the front door—the one my sister got me from her trip to Santa Fe back in 2018—the very second I walk in the house. Never lose 'em.\n\nDoctor: Have you had any recent physical health problems, head injuries, or new medications that started around the same time this difficulty with your thoughts began?\n\nPatient: Physical health problems or head injuries? No, no, nothing like that. I haven't hit my head or been in any accidents. The last time I had any kind of real physical issue was... oh, gosh, it must have been three years ago when I pulled a muscle in my lower back trying to lift a display case that was way too heavy for one person. But that healed up just fine after a few weeks of physical therapy and some muscle relaxers they gave me at the time. \n\nAnd as for new medications, no, nothing new there either. I've been taking the same blood pressure medication—Lisinopril, 10 milligrams, a little pink pill—every morning with my breakfast for the last five years. My doctor, Dr. Evans, he's a great guy, always says my pressure is right where it needs to be, usually around 120 over 80, give or take a point or two depending on if I've had my morning coffee yet. I take a multivitamin, too, just a generic one from the pharmacy down the street, the one with extra vitamin D because I don't get out in the sun much working retail all day. \n\nBut no new pills, no changes to my diet, no falls, no bumps on the head. I haven't even had a cold lately. I'm generally pretty healthy for a guy pushing sixty, you know? I try to eat right, mostly chicken and vegetables, maybe a steak once a month as a treat. So, no, there's no obvious physical reason why my thoughts are suddenly getting all tangled up like this. It just sort of... started happening on its own, without any warning or any changes in my routine. I wish it was as simple as a new medication causing a side effect, because then I could just stop taking it and go back to normal, but unfortunately, that's just not the case. It's just my brain doing this... this weird thing all by itself.\n\nDoctor: When your mind is racing and you're trying to explain things to your team, do you find yourself feeling a sense of overwhelming worry, dread, or apprehension about the future or about things going wrong?\n\nPatient: Worry? Dread? Oh, no, no, it's not like I'm having a panic attack or anything like that. I don't feel like the sky is falling or that the store is going to burn down. It's not a fearful feeling at all, really. I mean, sure, I want things to go right because I take pride in my work—I've been managing teams for over fifteen years, and I like a tight ship. Well, it’s funny you ask that, because I actually carry a planner with me everywhere. But recently, when I try to sit down and explain the inventory numbers for the week, or... or even just go over the weekend schedule with the staff, it's like my brain just takes off in a dozen different directions at once. \n\nI'll start talking about the stock levels, and then suddenly I'm talking about the delivery trucks, which reminds me that Thursday is usually a heavy delivery day, but Thursday is also when we have the church grill out back, and then I start thinking about the way my boss sounded when he asked me about the grill last week—his tone was just... off, you know? They have these blank looks on their faces, like they can't follow a single word I'm saying. It's frustrating because it all makes perfect sense in my head, but when it comes out, it's like a tangled ball of yarn and they just... they don't get it. Oh, no, no. Definitely not energetic. If anything, Dr. Smith, it's quite the opposite when it comes to my physical energy. You see, being on the retail floor all day at my age—I'm 59 now—it really takes a toll on the joints. I'm on my feet from the moment I clock in. Well, technically I get there about fifteen minutes early, around 7:15 AM, just to walk the perimeter and check the endcaps before the doors open, but by the time I get home at night, I am absolutely wiped out. I have this brown leather recliner in my living room, great lumbar support, and the second I sit down in it, I just deflate like an old tire. \n\nSo there's certainly no unusual burst of energy going on. And as for sleep... well, I definitely still need my sleep. I try my hardest to get my full eight hours every single night. I crave it. I certainly don't feel like I can just skip it or run on fumes. \n\nIf I get anything less than seven hours, I'm dragging my feet the whole next day. Like last Tuesday, the neighbor's golden retriever was barking at all hours—nice dog usually, but he just wouldn't quit at the fence—and I only got maybe five hours of rest. I see the truck manifest, I know we have three pallets of seasonal goods that need to be broken down, I know the registers need till audits... but when I open my mouth to tell them, the words just bottleneck. \n\nIt's frustrating, certainly. Extremely frustrating. It makes me feel embarrassed, like I look foolish in front of my own staff, you know? But it's not dread. I'm not standing there thinking something terrible is about to happen to me or to them. I'm just standing there thinking, \"Come on, Frank, just say the sentence. Just tell Dave to take the pallet jack to aisle four.\" But instead, it comes out all jumbled, like I'm trying to talk around a mouthful of marbles. So, no, it's not an overwhelming worry or apprehension about the future. It's just an overwhelming frustration with my own mouth in that exact moment.\n\nDoctor: Does this same feeling of your words becoming a 'tangled ball of yarn' happen when you are talking to friends or family in a relaxed setting, or does it only seem to occur when you are under pressure at work?\n\nPatient: Well, that’s exactly it, doctor, that’s actually the main reason I finally decided I needed to come in and see somebody about this. I originally thought it was just the stress of the retail environment, you know? Because it definitely happens at the store. I'll be standing there trying to explain the inventory numbers for the new quarter, or maybe I’m just trying to lay out the weekend schedule for the floor staff—which is always a headache anyway because nobody ever wants to work the Sunday morning opening shift—and the words just get entirely derailed. \n\nBut then I realized it’s not just work. It’s happening everywhere, even when I'm completely relaxed. I’ll start out trying to talk about something simple, and then my words start jumping all over the place without my permission. Trucks to Thursdays to the church grill to my boss's tone, all strung together in the same breath like it's supposed to make perfect sense. They just stop, and they stare at me, and they get this deeply confused look on their faces... people just look at me like they absolutely can’t follow what I’m saying. It's happening when I'm just trying to have a normal, relaxed conversation, too, and it's making it nearly impossible to just sit down and talk to people without feeling like I'm speaking a foreign language.\n\nDoctor: When you try to write down your thoughts or tasks in your planner, do you find that your writing also becomes jumbled and disorganized, or is it only your spoken words that seem to get tangled?\n\nPatient: Writing it down? Talking behind my back? Sabotage? Oh, heavens, no. No, no, no, nothing like that. 

I mean... look, retail is retail, right? Any time you have an employee breakroom, you're going to have a little bit of gossip. That’s just human nature. You get a bunch of twenty-somethings working for near minimum wage, they're going to complain about management, they're going to complain about their hours, they're going to complain about the customers. That's just the reality of the business, and after doing this for as long as I have, you develop a pretty thick skin about the normal day-to-day chatter. 

But as far as them actually plotting against me? Or intentionally trying to sabotage my work? Not at all. I don't believe that for a second. Take Dave, for instance, the cashier I was mentioning earlier. Dave is a good kid. He’s been on the front end for almost two years now, and he’s just trying to pay his way through community college. He doesn't care enough about the corporate ladder to try and sabotage a fifty-nine-year-old floor supervisor. Honestly, none of them do. They just want to punch in, do their eight hours, and punch out. 

When I'm having those moments—when I'm just standing there in the main action alley, completely stuck, staring at that weekend schedule on my clipboard like it's written in ancient Greek—they aren't whispering about how to ruin my career. They aren't scheming. They're just... waiting. They're probably just thinking, "Come on, old man, just tell me if I'm on register four or if I'm pulling pallets from receiving so I can get this shift over with." 

It's not malicious. If anything, they're probably just annoyed because my delay means their fifteen-minute break gets pushed back. So, no, I don't have any grand theories about them being out to get me or talking about me behind my back. The only person sabotaging my work right now is me, honestly, with this... this mental roadblock, or whatever it is that keeps happening. It's all on my end. The associates are just innocent bystanders caught in the crossfire of my brain stalling out while I'm supposed to be delegating tasks. So I definitely don't blame them, and I certainly don't think they're out to get me.

Hidden meaning? Secret messages in the... in the products? Oh, no. No, definitely not. 

You see, in retail—especially at our level, with the corporate structure we have—there is absolutely no room for creativity on the shelves to begin with. It’s all dictated by the planograms. They're just following the binder. It’s supposed to be two facings of chicken noodle, three facings of tomato, all the labels facing out, pulled flush to the front edge of the shelf—what we call "zoning" or "facing" the store. 

I mean, if I walk down an aisle and see that someone put the generic store-brand cereal where the name-brand is supposed to go, I don't look at that and think it's a secret code directed at me. I just think... well, I just think it's laziness, or that they weren't paying attention to the barcodes on the shelf tags, and now I'm going to have to go over there and have them fix it. Which, honestly, is part of why I get so frustrated when I have those moments where I just freeze up with my clipboard. Because I know the shelves need to be zoned, I know the district manager might be doing a walkthrough on Tuesday, and instead of directing my team to fix the shelves, I just... I just stand there. 

But no, I don't look at a display of canned goods or the battery rack I keep pacing past and think it means something special. A battery is just a battery. A crooked box of cereal is just a crooked box of cereal. There's no secret code going on. The associates are just trying to get the freight off the pallets and onto the floor before the morning rush hits, that's all there is to it. If they actually wanted to send me a message, they’d just write it on a sticky note and leave it on the desk in the back office, you know? So, no, nothing like that at all. Just the standard corporate layouts.

The ink on the page usually makes sense. \n\nBut the second I have to actually *talk* about what I just wrote... well, that’s exactly what I was just telling you about. That’s the whole reason I came in here today. I'll have that planner right there in my hand, open to the right page, and I'll try to explain those inventory numbers or that weekend schedule to the floor staff, and instead of just saying what I wrote, my mouth just takes off on its own. \n\nLike I was just saying, it doesn't matter if it's written down right in front of me, my words still start jumping from the delivery trucks, to Thursdays, to that heavy church grill, all the way to my boss’s tone of voice on a conference call. It just completely detaches from what's on the paper. I could have it bullet-pointed perfectly, color-coded even, but when I try to speak it out loud, the words just scatter everywhere. And then I'm left standing there holding my nice leather planner while people just look at me like they absolutely can’t follow a single thing I’m saying. So, I suppose the writing itself is mostly okay, as long as I have quiet time to do it, but it doesn't do me any good once I actually have to open my mouth. The talking is where all the wires get crossed.\n\nDoctor: If I were to ask you to repeat the phrase 'The quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog' back to me right now, would you be able to do that clearly, or would the words get jumbled in the same way?\n\nPatient: Well, \"the quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog\"—I mean, I could probably say that right now without a hitch. Let's see... \"The quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog.\" See? Clear as day. But, doctor, with all due respect, that’s just a memorized trick from middle school typing class. It's when I have to explain the actual inventory numbers for the store, or when I'm trying to lay out that weekend schedule for the staff. \n\nI know I keep bringing up those same examples, but it's just the absolute perfect illustration of how bad this has gotten. My tongue and my lips, they work perfectly fine. It's like my brain is just pulling files from completely different cabinets and throwing them all on the desk at the exact same time. \n\nLike I keep telling you—and I know I must sound like a broken record by now, going on and on about the same exact situations, but I really just want you to understand because this is exactly why I finally came in here to see you—when I try to explain those inventory numbers or that weekend schedule, my mouth is doing its job perfectly. It jumps right from the schedule to those delivery trucks, and then to Thursdays, and then to that heavy church grill, and then right into my boss’s tone of voice. \n\nIt’s all happening up here, in the thoughts.
